replies.author: jamurai
replies.body:
For assets: you can find them in a store for purchase (unity store), or you can generate with tripo (my favorite). For gpt models: they do a great job at image gen and it’s easy to set up a pipeline for GPT images into tripo assets (either upload yourself or have Sol walk you through the process of setting up the API/CLI for it to do it automatically. Just note there is different payment for web vs cli). 

For map layouts: have it do research first. Or provide it with examples of games you like. I’m working through this now actually for a city game. I had it research real city data and it’s iterating by creating SVG maps of it before implementing. Have it start by focusing on the large shapes first, put those on “paper” in an SVG and then iterate with it on details filling in the map section by section

replies.author: Mammoth-Range-4219
replies.body: I've been a producer in the gaming industry for 20 years and I can tell you this: ai can be a TOOL, but you CAN'T give it the wheels and think it knows level design, even the slightest bit. Of course in the recent years we've been asked to explore AI, I had to do reports and findings, and it's (as of yet) NOT a magical "studio-all-in-one". It's good at EXECUTING pure mathematical outputs, but it's VERY bad at anything creative; what moves humans; what makes them laugh or cry or angry. As for now, a good level design, a good story, heck a good joke or even just a pun, is falling flat coming from AI. And it really looks like you just told it to "make a map with a dirty road and houses scattered", it can NEVER, again, as of yet, produce the level design needed for your game to come somewhat close to something enticing people would want to play. And if you're not the creative type, this is what you need to work on or this isn't going anywhere

comments.author: Impetigocheez
comments.body:
I've been developing games with AI for most of this year, and I've probably started or worked on eight different projects at this point, with one released on Steam. I'm still learning a tremendous amount, but there are definitely some lessons I've picked up that I wish I'd understood when I started.

**The number one thing I'd recommend is having a game design bible before you start.**

I'm talking about a living document that establishes your game's design philosophy, objectives, controls, core gameplay loop, and at least 4–5 major systems you want to implement. You should understand conceptually how those systems are supposed to work, how they interact, and what you're actually trying to accomplish with them.

But here's the important part: **your game design bible should evolve with the game.**

I've been working on a Vietnam-era FPS/RPG for around four months now, and the game I'm developing today is substantially different from what I originally envisioned.

Initially, it was basically a Vietnam War simulator. You existed in the world, could move around, fight, and interact with things, but there weren't really missions or objectives. Eventually, I realized that while the simulation was interesting, it wasn't necessarily that fun.

So I started incorporating elements from a Vietnam War horror comic I've been writing, including psychological horror and some pretty disturbing themes. Eventually, I felt like I was borrowing too directly from my own story, so I pulled back and started exploring something different.

Now I'm developing this combination of *Deus Ex*\-style RPG gameplay and *Call of Duty*\-style military missions, with the idea that your actions in one part of the game will influence the other. That's still something I'm developing and haven't fully proven mechanically, but it's the direction I'm exploring.

The point is that **you need a vision, but you also need to be willing to change that vision when you discover something isn't working.**

Another enormous lesson is getting your artwork and visual direction established early.

I'm an artist by trade, and I've built almost my entire asset library using Blender and MCP tools. One of the biggest bottlenecks early on was constantly bouncing between creating artwork and implementing gameplay systems.

The more artwork you can prepare beforehand, the easier everything becomes. And if you're working on multiple projects with similar aesthetics or mechanics, those assets start becoming incredibly valuable.

I've worked on RPGs, shooters, and strategy games this year, and many of them share the same general visual language and underlying systems. Something I build for one project can often be modified and implemented into another.

**The work starts compounding on itself.**

That said, your artwork is never really finished either. I've probably redesigned the characters in my Vietnam game 15 times at this point, and I'm still improving them.

I once heard a developer say something along the lines of your artwork will stay the way it is until you're sick of looking at it, and then you'll improve it. That's been pretty accurate to my experience.

Coming from an art background, I understand that what you start with isn't necessarily what you're going to end up with. Sometimes you need to see something implemented before you realize what needs to change.

**Memory and documentation are also extremely important.**

I initially experimented with Beads for tracking development in Claude, but eventually ran into some pretty frustrating context drift. I'd spend enormous amounts of time updating records, only for them to become outdated and cause the AI to revisit problems we'd already solved.

Now I maintain living documentation directly inside my projects, and whenever I'm ending a context session, I ask Claude to prepare a handoff note explaining what we've accomplished and what we're continuing to work on.

Combined with improvements to my memory setup, this has made development substantially more consistent.

**Another thing that's changed dramatically is how much work I'm willing to delegate.**

When I first started, I was doing everything one tiny step at a time. Make a box move. Add a mechanic. Make something shoot. Then figure out what to do next.

My first major project took around two months, and progress felt painfully slow.

Now I regularly have Claude working overnight on my computer with access to the actual project files. Sometimes I'll have it help develop a 100-step overnight plan, and other times I'll ask it to identify 100 things that would move the project closer to a playable demo.

Because we've already spent so much time establishing the game's systems, aesthetics, design philosophy, and things I specifically don't want, I can give it considerably more freedom to work independently.

I don't necessarily need to dictate every individual implementation anymore. I can establish the direction and let it figure out how to accomplish things, then review what it's done and correct anything that isn't working.

That doesn't mean blindly trusting everything it produces. Early on, I made that mistake constantly. The AI would enthusiastically agree to implement all sorts of things, create folders and plans, and then sometimes accomplish very little of what it claimed.

I've learned to distinguish between the AI saying something is finished and actually seeing it function in the game.

I'll admit my playtesting process could still be better. Sometimes I get so caught up in developing new features that I'll go weeks without properly playing the game. A lot of my current issues are visual, like animations behaving incorrectly or models floating, but I know that testing more frequently would help catch problems earlier.

As far as models go, I primarily use Claude with Blender MCP tools. I generally prefer stronger models and higher reasoning effort for complex work, while delegating simpler implementation tasks where it makes sense.

I've also started experimenting with studying the construction of older games to better understand how developers accomplished certain things, especially with the technical limitations of the late '90s and early 2000s.

**But probably the biggest thing I want to emphasize is that AI development still requires an enormous amount of work from you.**

I'm spending something like 60 hours a week developing, designing, reviewing, and directing these projects.

AI has made it possible for me to pursue ideas that would've been substantially more difficult to accomplish on my own, but it's not doing all the creative thinking for me.

You have to understand what you're trying to make. You have to play your game, recognize what isn't fun, rethink systems, improve the artwork, and constantly steer the project toward something better.

And you have to accept that sometimes an idea you spent weeks developing just isn't going to work the way you imagined.

I've only released one game on Steam so far, and it wasn't some massive success. But I've learned an incredible amount from developing all these projects, and I'm hoping to release at least two more by the end of next year.

I think that's another important part of the process. You have to actually keep making things.

**AI isn't a magic button where you type "make me a game" and expect something great to come out. It's a tool that lets you accomplish a lot more when you're willing to put in the effort to direct it.**

The more I've learned about planning, art production, managing context, and developing systems, the more useful the AI has become.

You still have to be the designer. You still have to have the vision. And you still have to put in the work.

Just keep making things, dude.

replies.author: AtumTheCreator
replies.body:
Its crazy that we live in a world where typos and grammer errors are becoming more widely acceptable than perfect writing.

When I was growing up we strived to have perfect writing. Even online, where one little mistake would get you flamed for incorrect grammer.

Now, we have it...in a very obvious style and tone, but we have it.

A lot of non native speakers can't convey messages on English correctly, or things get lost in translation. Google translate never fully solved that.

I don't mind the use of AI in general. Think of it like this, in American schools we used to teach cursive. It was a form of your own individual artistic expression. It was replaced by the computer and typing, mostly.

Same thing is happening now. Our forms of artistic expression are being taken from us. It sucks, but we move forward, and find our happiness in different places.

replies.author: romansamurai
replies.body:
Few things that I feel are key that you described that I’ve been doing myself

GDD - Game Design Document. Alamo known as Bible. 100% key.

Handoff notes.  Can’t stress this enough. Have Claude create this for new Claude sessions for hand off between accounts or devices.  Have a separate work done document where it can log what was done with versioning as well as new changes to be done next session in a separate doc so Claude doesn’t have to read the GDD again each new session unless necessary etc.

Oh and GitHub for back up. Everything gets pushed to GitHub.

And yeah. Because the game art direction, design and systems are well documented and established and safeguards are in place I can have it run a dozen agents testing, writing, building and iterating things at night for me to review on the morning. It will auto resume each time it hits the 5 hr limit too.

And yes. Easily spending 4-5 hrs a day (with a full time job, family and home) during that week and upwards to 12 a day on weekend working on this.  

I feel at this point I am just a managing director. Responsible for art direction, systems and reviewing my team’s work. I had Claude running 216 tasks at once this week at one point. I can’t imagine how many people you’d need on a team to do that amount of work in that amount of time.

replies.author: Emotional-Cut2952
replies.body:
what? respectfully, gpt has the most precision in coding, claude has good ideation, creativity, design and architecture - this is factual, it's recognized by both teams that gpt models excute with surprising precision - sol 6.1 precision beats opus 5.5, but opus 5.5 has agentic autonomy that is better than sol or even astra and can design the best architures and specs,

I've been using opus + sonnet + haiku combo for a while hammering away at it day Mon - Friday.

My flow:

* Opus creates architecture and spec  
* using Sonnet writes src + tests 
* Haiku gathers initial documentaiton/context for opus; it then runs tests , reads reports 
* Opus review  source and tests implementation against architecture and spec

Hand off order:

Opus -> haiku (research) -> opus (architecture/spec) -> sonnet (src + tests)

sonnet (src + tests) -> haiku (runs tests) -> sonnet (review issues) -> haiku (rerun tests) -> rinse and repeate

I have /codex-review /codex-rescue  among others to use when im getting near my session limits on claude where it willl invoke sol in the place of sonnet and luna in the place of haiku, sometimes i just switch straight to my codex app and give it the last few messages from my claude chat, i.e. handoff looks something like:

Sol  (review + patch src / tests) -> luna 6 (run test) -> sol (review issues) -> luna 6 (rerun tests)

each claude / codex is on their cheapest \~ $20 monthly subs

comments.author: Comprehensive_Rush66
comments.body:
Astra / Sol are terrible IMO. I've wasted hours with both of them and the outputs are poor even on High / xHigh settings — which also completely drain your 7-day usage window in a matter of hours. 

Opus 5.5 High / xHigh have been fantastic for game dev. I made this with Opus 5.5 in 5-days (all assets generated locally via open weight models: art, animation, sound): [astra-black.com](http://astra-black.com)

Working on a 3D game now and tried to use Astra on that and the output was atroscious. Completely lacked any understanding of visual fidelity, gameplay mechanics, realtime rendering that looks presentable or with a higher production value. 

OpenAI's frontier models are far behind at this point in time and seem to consume much more usage with 2x poorer output in my experience.
